newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian farmers hit hard by funds fiasco and cold.
newsitem.headline: Albanian farmers hit hard by funds fiasco and cold.

text.p: Albanian farmers are struggling to produce a reasonable crop this year, hit by unseasonally cold weather and the collapse of get-rich-quick pyramid funds that left them with no money for fertilisers.
Hunched over her rusty hoe, Bukuri Gici drags the soil, preparing to plant tomatoes for the third time this year.
The cold destroyed earlier attempts but Gici refuses to admit defeat. Her crop must succeed.

Gici is one of thousands of Albanian farmers who invested in the pyramid scams that collapsed in January, triggering a wave of violence across the impoverished Balkan nation and the resignation of the Democratic Party government.
"The little money we had ($2,000) we invested in the pyramid funds and we have lost it all," said Gici, 38, who is struggling to feed her two children and invalid mother-in-law.
"We cannot afford to buy fertiliser now to help our crops. We need this crop to eat. We won't make any money this year."
Gici said the weather was the worst in six years in Albania's key farming area, the lowland Myzeqe basin between Lushnje and Vlore in the southwest, known as Albania's granary.

"From the time land was made private, we have not had such a bad year," said Gici, whose family received 0.8 hectares at Karbunare in the Myzeqe basin when land was divided into plots after the 1990 fall of communism.
Agricultural production in Albania is limited.

Most farming is done manually as the 70 percent of Albania's 3.4 million people that live in rural areas of Europe's poorest state cannot afford machinery. Equipment used during the communist era is outdated or broken.
The agricultural sector was struggling to meet domestic demand before the recent crisis -- and now the combination of cold weather and lack of money has hit 1997 production.
However wheat output this year was expected to exceed the 316,000 tonnes produced in 1996, Agriculture Ministry spokesman Aleksander Mari told Reuters.
"About 130,000 hectares have been planted to wheat this year which is 12,000 hectares more than last year," Mari said.
"The spring has not been too hot like last year when some of the crop burnt and we hope for more production," he said, adding that the harvest will start in late June.
Wheat production in Albania has fallen sharply since the end of communism. State and cooperative farms produced 630,000 tonnes of wheat in 1990.

Many of Albania's 38 industrial scale flour mills are closed, with too little domestic output for operations. Mills still working are near harbours and process imported wheat. Albania imports about 140,000 tonnes a year.
About 580,154 hectares of Albania's 702,005 hectares of arable land, or 20 percent of total area, are cultivated but production is falling annually.
In 1990 Albania produced about 3,000 tonnes of sunflower seed but output has fallen to 1,000 tonnes in recent years.
Olive production has continued to fluctuate between 20,000 and 40,000 tonnes a year. Mari said about 8,000 hectares would be planted with tobacco this year.
Myzeqe basin farmers also grow beans, carrots, potatoes, and watermelons but the cold has hit their crops.
"Our lives depend totally on the weather," said Sofia Bardhi, a 40-year-old mother of three, whose family owns two hectares of farmland near Kolonje village in the Myzeqe basin.
"Everyone around here lost money. We lost about $3,000. We even sold one of our two cows and put that money in the fund.
"Now we have planted every centimetre of our land. We just have to hope."
